blocks.body:
List the powers of $3$ modulo $7$: $3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1$, and then the cycle repeats. Every nonzero residue shows up. The powers of $2$ modulo $7$ behave differently: $2, 4, 1, 2, 4, 1, \dots$, a cycle of length $3$ that misses half the residues.

The length of such a cycle is the order of the base. A base whose powers reach every invertible residue is a primitive root. When a primitive root $g$ exists, every invertible residue can be written as $g^k$, so multiplication of residues becomes addition of exponents, much as logarithms turn products into sums. This lesson proves that every prime has a primitive root and explains why some moduli have none.

blocks.title: Order of a residue
blocks.body:
Let $n \ge 1$ and $\gcd(a, n) = 1$. The order of $a$ modulo $n$, written $\operatorname{ord}_n(a)$, is the least positive integer $k$ with $a^k \equiv 1 \pmod n$.

The order exists because $a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod n$ by [[fermat-euler|Euler's theorem]]. It is the length of the repeating cycle $a, a^2, a^3, \dots$ modulo $n$.

blocks.title: Basic properties of the order
blocks.body:
Let $k = \operatorname{ord}_n(a)$. Then:

1. $a^m \equiv 1 \pmod n$ if and only if $k \mid m$. In particular $k \mid \varphi(n)$, and $k \mid p - 1$ when $n = p$ is prime.
2. $a^i \equiv a^j \pmod n$ if and only if $i \equiv j \pmod k$.
3. For any integer $j \ge 0$, $\operatorname{ord}_n(a^j) = \dfrac{k}{\gcd(k, j)}$.

1. Divide: $m = qk + r$ with $0 \le r < k$. Then $a^m = (a^k)^q a^r \equiv a^r$. If $a^m \equiv 1$, then $a^r \equiv 1$ with $r < k$, which forces $r = 0$ by minimality of $k$. The converse is clear. Since $a^{\varphi(n)} \equiv 1$, we get $k \mid \varphi(n)$.

2. Because $a$ is invertible, $a^i \equiv a^j$ (say with $i \ge j$) is equivalent to $a^{i-j} \equiv 1$, which by part 1 means $k \mid i - j$.

3. By part 1, $(a^j)^m \equiv 1$ if and only if $k \mid jm$. Write $g = \gcd(k, j)$. The condition $k \mid jm$ is equivalent to $\frac kg \mid \frac jg m$, and since $\frac kg$ and $\frac jg$ are coprime this is equivalent to $\frac kg \mid m$. The least such positive $m$ is $k/g$.

blocks.title: Primitive root
blocks.body:
An integer $g$ coprime to $n$ is a primitive root modulo $n$ if $\operatorname{ord}_n(g) = \varphi(n)$. Then $g^0, g^1, \dots, g^{\varphi(n)-1}$ are pairwise incongruent (by part 2 above), so they are all the invertible residues modulo $n$.

For a prime $p$, a primitive root has order $p-1$, and every nonzero residue modulo $p$ is a power of it.

blocks.title: A polynomial fact
blocks.body:
The existence proof for primes rests on one fact about polynomials.

Lagrange's theorem. If $p$ is prime and $f(x)$ is a polynomial with integer coefficients of degree $d \ge 0$ whose leading coefficient is not divisible by $p$, then $f(x) \equiv 0 \pmod p$ has at most $d$ solutions modulo $p$.

Proof by induction on $d$. For $d = 0$, $f$ is a constant not divisible by $p$ and has no roots. If $d \ge 1$ and $r$ is a root, polynomial division gives $f(x) = (x - r)q(x) + f(r)$, where $q$ has degree $d - 1$ and the same leading coefficient. Since $f(r) \equiv 0$, we get $f(x) \equiv (x - r)q(x)$ for all integers $x$. Any other root $s \not\equiv r$ satisfies $(s - r)q(s) \equiv 0$. Since $p$ is prime and $p \nmid s - r$, we get $q(s) \equiv 0$. By induction $q$ has at most $d - 1$ roots, so $f$ has at most $d$.

Primality matters: modulo $8$ the quadratic $x^2 - 1$ has four roots, $1, 3, 5, 7$.

blocks.title: Existence of primitive roots modulo a prime
blocks.body:
Every prime $p$ has a primitive root. More precisely, for every $d \mid p - 1$ there are exactly $\varphi(d)$ residues of order $d$ modulo $p$. In particular there are $\varphi(p-1)$ primitive roots, and if $g$ is one of them, then $k \mapsto g^k$ gives an isomorphism

$$(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^\times \cong \mathbb Z/(p-1)\mathbb Z.$$

For $d \mid p - 1$, let $\psi(d)$ be the number of residues in $\{1, \dots, p-1\}$ of order exactly $d$.

Suppose $\psi(d) \ge 1$, and let $a$ have order $d$. The residues $1, a, a^2, \dots, a^{d-1}$ are distinct, and each is a root of $x^d - 1$, since $(a^j)^d = (a^d)^j \equiv 1$. By Lagrange's theorem $x^d - 1$ has at most $d$ roots, so these are all of them. Any element of order $d$ is a root of $x^d - 1$, so it is one of the $a^j$. By part 3 of the previous theorem, $a^j$ has order $d/\gcd(d, j)$, which equals $d$ exactly when $\gcd(d, j) = 1$. So $\psi(d) = \varphi(d)$.

We have shown $\psi(d) \in \{0, \varphi(d)\}$ for each $d \mid p - 1$. Every residue has some order dividing $p - 1$, so

$$\sum_{d \mid p-1}\psi(d) = p - 1 = \sum_{d \mid p-1}\varphi(d),$$

where the second equality is Gauss's identity from [[arithmetic-functions]]. Since $\psi(d) \le \varphi(d)$ term by term and the sums agree, $\psi(d) = \varphi(d)$ for every $d$. In particular $\psi(p-1) = \varphi(p-1) \ge 1$.

For the isomorphism: the map $k \bmod (p-1) \mapsto g^k \bmod p$ is well defined and injective by part 2 of the previous theorem, surjective because $g$ is a primitive root, and it turns addition of exponents into multiplication: $g^{k+l} = g^k g^l$.

blocks.title: Finding primitive roots, and indices
blocks.body:
In practice we look for a primitive root by trying $g = 2, 3, 5, \dots$. Testing one candidate does not require computing all $p - 1$ powers.

Test. $g$ is a primitive root modulo $p$ if and only if $g^{(p-1)/q} \not\equiv 1 \pmod p$ for every prime $q \mid p - 1$.

The reason: if the order $k$ of $g$ is a proper divisor of $p - 1$, then $(p-1)/k$ has some prime factor $q$, so $k \mid (p-1)/q$ and $g^{(p-1)/q} \equiv 1$. Conversely, if $g$ has order $p - 1$, no smaller positive exponent gives $1$.

Once $g$ is fixed, the exponent $k$ with $a \equiv g^k$ is called the index or discrete logarithm of $a$, written $\operatorname{ind}_g a$. It is defined modulo $p - 1$, and it satisfies $\operatorname{ind}_g(ab) \equiv \operatorname{ind}_g a + \operatorname{ind}_g b \pmod{p-1}$. Many questions about the multiplicative structure become linear algebra modulo $p - 1$. For instance, when $p \nmid a$, the congruence $x^m \equiv a \pmod p$ becomes $m\cdot\operatorname{ind}_g x \equiv \operatorname{ind}_g a \pmod{p-1}$, a [[mod-inverse|linear congruence]].

blocks.title: Which moduli have primitive roots
blocks.body: A primitive root modulo $n$ exists if and only if $n$ is $1$, $2$, $4$, $p^k$ or $2p^k$, where $p$ is an odd prime and $k \ge 1$.

blocks.title: Why some moduli have no primitive root
blocks.body:
The "only if" direction is short. Suppose $n = ab$ with $\gcd(a, b) = 1$ and $a, b > 2$. Then $\varphi(a)$ and $\varphi(b)$ are both even, so $L = \operatorname{lcm}(\varphi(a), \varphi(b)) \le \varphi(a)\varphi(b)/2 = \varphi(n)/2$. For any $x$ coprime to $n$, Euler's theorem gives $x^L \equiv 1$ modulo both $a$ and $b$, hence modulo $n$. So every order is at most $\varphi(n)/2$, and there is no primitive root. This rules out every $n$ with two different odd prime factors, and every $n = 2^j m$ with $j \ge 2$ and odd $m > 1$.

Powers of $2$ from $8$ on fail for a different reason. Every odd $x$ satisfies $x^2 \equiv 1 \pmod 8$. Squaring repeatedly, if $x^{2^{j}} = 1 + 2^{j+2}t$, then $x^{2^{j+1}} = 1 + 2^{j+3}t + 2^{2j+4}t^2 \equiv 1 \pmod{2^{j+3}}$. So $x^{2^{k-2}} \equiv 1 \pmod{2^k}$ for $k \ge 3$, and orders never reach $\varphi(2^k) = 2^{k-1}$.

For the "if" direction, let $p$ be an odd prime. One lifts a primitive root from $p$ to $p^2$ and then to every $p^k$. If $g$ is a primitive root mod $p$, then either $g$ or $g + p$ is a primitive root mod $p^2$, and any primitive root mod $p^2$ is one mod every $p^k$. Here oddness of $p$ is essential: $3$ is a primitive root modulo $4$ but not modulo $8$. Finally, an odd primitive root mod $p^k$ is also one mod $2p^k$ (if $g$ is even, use $g + p^k$ instead). We do not give the details here; they are in the references and in [[hensel]]. The lifting step is genuinely needed: $10$ is a primitive root modulo $487$, but $10^{486} \equiv 1 \pmod{487^2}$, so $10$ is not a primitive root modulo $487^2$.
Find the orders of $2$ and $3$ modulo $13$, and list all primitive roots modulo $13$.
blocks.solution:
Powers of $2$ modulo $13$: $2, 4, 8, 3, 6, 12, \dots$ Since $2^6 \equiv 12 \equiv -1$, we get $2^{12} \equiv 1$, while $2^4 = 16 \equiv 3$ and $2^6 \equiv -1$ are not $1$. The possible orders are divisors of $12$, and the test with $q = 2, 3$ checks $2^{6} \not\equiv 1$ and $2^{4} \not\equiv 1$. So $\operatorname{ord}_{13}(2) = 12$, and $2$ is a primitive root.

Powers of $3$: $3, 9, 27 \equiv 1$. So $\operatorname{ord}_{13}(3) = 3$.

The primitive roots are $2^j$ with $\gcd(j, 12) = 1$, that is, $j = 1, 5, 7, 11$: $2^1 = 2$, $2^5 = 32 \equiv 6$, $2^7 = 128 \equiv 11$, $2^{11} = 2048 \equiv 7$. So the primitive roots modulo $13$ are $2, 6, 7, 11$, and there are $\varphi(12) = 4$ of them, as predicted.

blocks.body: Find the least primitive root modulo $23$.
blocks.solution:
$p - 1 = 22 = 2 \cdot 11$, so $g$ is a primitive root exactly when $g^{11} \not\equiv 1$ and $g^{2} \not\equiv 1 \pmod{23}$.

$g = 2$: $2^{11} = 2048 = 23 \cdot 89 + 1$, so $2^{11} \equiv 1$. Not a primitive root.

$g = 3$: $3^3 = 27 \equiv 4$, $3^9 \equiv 4^3 = 64 \equiv 18$, $3^{11} \equiv 18 \cdot 9 = 162 = 7 \cdot 23 + 1 \equiv 1$. Not a primitive root.

$g = 4 = 2^2$: its order divides that of $2$, so it is not one.

$g = 5$: $5^2 = 25 \equiv 2 \not\equiv 1$. Then $5^{11} = 5^8 \cdot 5^2 \cdot 5 \equiv 16 \cdot 2 \cdot 5 = 160 \equiv -1$, using $5^4 \equiv 4$ and $5^8 \equiv 16$. So $5^{11} \not\equiv 1$.

The least primitive root modulo $23$ is $5$.

blocks.body:
Let $p$ be a prime and $m$ a positive integer. Prove that

$$1^m + 2^m + \dots + (p-1)^m \equiv \begin{cases} -1 \pmod p & \text{if } p - 1 \mid m,\\ 0 \pmod p & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$
blocks.solution:
Let $g$ be a primitive root modulo $p$. As $k$ runs over $1, \dots, p-1$, the residue $k$ runs over $g^0, g^1, \dots, g^{p-2}$. So

$$S = \sum_{k=1}^{p-1}k^m \equiv \sum_{j=0}^{p-2}\bigl(g^m\bigr)^j \pmod p.$$

If $p - 1 \mid m$, then $g^m \equiv 1$, every term is $1$, and $S \equiv p - 1 \equiv -1$.

Otherwise $g^m \not\equiv 1$, because the order of $g$ is $p - 1$ and $p - 1 \nmid m$. Then $g^m - 1$ is invertible modulo $p$, and the geometric sum gives

$$(g^m - 1)\,S \equiv (g^m)^{p-1} - 1 = (g^{p-1})^m - 1 \equiv 0 \pmod p.$$

Cancelling the invertible factor gives $S \equiv 0$.

blocks.body: Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $q$ be a prime dividing $2^p - 1$. Prove that $q \equiv 1 \pmod{2p}$. Check this on $2^{11} - 1$.
blocks.solution:
Since $2^p \equiv 1 \pmod q$, the order of $2$ modulo $q$ divides $p$, so it is $1$ or $p$. It is not $1$, since $2^1 - 1 = 1$ is not divisible by $q$. So $\operatorname{ord}_q(2) = p$, and since the order divides $q - 1$, we get $p \mid q - 1$. Also $q$ is odd, because $2^p - 1$ is odd. So $2 \mid q - 1$, and as $p$ is odd, $2p \mid q - 1$.

For $p = 11$: $2^{11} - 1 = 2047 = 23 \cdot 89$, and indeed $23 = 2 \cdot 11 + 1$ and $89 = 4 \cdot 22 + 1$. This argument goes back to Fermat. It makes searching for factors of Mersenne numbers much faster, because only primes of the form $2pk + 1$ need to be tried.

blocks.body:
- The order is only defined when $\gcd(a, n) = 1$; for example, no power of $2$ is $\equiv 1 \pmod 6$.
- The order divides $\varphi(n)$ but need not equal it. Euler's theorem gives an exponent that works, not the least one.
- Indices live modulo $p - 1$, not modulo $p$. Writing $\operatorname{ind}_g a$ as a residue mod $p$ is a common slip.
- Not every modulus has a primitive root: modulo $8$, the residues $1, 3, 5, 7$ all square to $1$.
- A primitive root modulo $p$ need not be a primitive root modulo $p^2$ (the example $10$ modulo $487$ above).
- The test "$g^{(p-1)/q} \not\equiv 1$" has to be applied for every prime $q \mid p - 1$. Checking only $q = 2$ is not enough.

With a primitive root in hand, $a = g^k$ is a square modulo $p$ exactly when $k$ is even. This gives Euler's criterion and is the starting point of [[quadratic-residues]]. Every [[dirichlet-characters|Dirichlet character]] modulo $p$ has the form $\chi(g^k) = e^{2\pi i jk/(p-1)}$ for some fixed $j \in \{0, 1, \dots, p-2\}$ (with $\chi(a) = 0$ when $p \mid a$), so characters are written down through indices. Orders of $a$ modulo primes control which primes divide $a^n - 1$, the theme of [[lte-zsigmondy]]. The cyclic structure is the arithmetic shadow of the roots of unity in [[cyclotomic]] fields, and the abstract statement that a finite subgroup of the multiplicative group of a field is cyclic belongs to [[groups]].

In cryptography, Diffie–Hellman key exchange publishes a prime $p$ and a primitive root $g$. Alice sends $g^a$, Bob sends $g^b$, and both compute $g^{ab}$. An eavesdropper sees only $g^a$ and $g^b$, and recovering $a$ is the discrete logarithm problem, believed to be hard for well-chosen large $p$ (see [[discrete-log]]). Artin conjectured that every integer $a$ other than $-1$ that is not a perfect square is a primitive root modulo infinitely many primes. (These are excluded because a square has order dividing $(p-1)/2$ and $-1$ has order $2$, so neither is a primitive root modulo any prime $p > 3$.) The conjecture is still not known for any single value of $a$, not even $a = 2$, but Hooley proved it in 1967 assuming a form of the [[grh|generalized Riemann hypothesis]] for certain number fields.

1. Find all primitive roots modulo $11$.
2. Let $g$ be a primitive root modulo an odd prime $p$. Show that $g^{(p-1)/2} \equiv -1 \pmod p$.
3. Using a primitive root, show that if $p \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ then $x^2 \equiv -1 \pmod p$ has a solution.
4. Show directly that there is no primitive root modulo $15$ by computing the orders of all eight invertible residues.
